title: Evolution of Import Documentation Requirements for Compliance and Audit
summary: The concept of 'import documents' has evolved from a basic requirement for customs clearance and agent authorization to a comprehensive, multi-layered framework for post-clearance audit (PCA) and regulatory compliance. Over time, the scope has expanded from simple submission of entry documents to detailed record-keeping, system-based audit trails, and specific evidentiary requirements for machinery installation and duty drawback.

evolution.scope: Expanded from clearance-stage submission to post-clearance audit and lifecycle verification.
evolution.structure: Shifted from manual/general submission to standardized, audit-ready reporting formats.
evolution.compliance: Increased focus on technical verification (chemical/surveyor reports) and system-based audit trails.

timeline.change: Established the foundational requirement for customs agents to submit authorization and entry documents.
Introduced mandatory technical documentation (literature, chemical analysis, packing lists) for verification of H.S. Codes and origin.
Defined exemptions from document submission for specific duty drawback schemes.
Formalized the transition to structured Transaction-Based and System-Based Audit documentation requirements.
Mandated specific document sets (LC, BL, IP, Surveyor reports) for post-import machinery installation verification.
Refined the audit documentation framework to include AEO status and specific organizational identifiers.

Customs Agent: A Customs Agent is required to perform various professional duties, including representing clients, verifying documents, and ensuring regulatory compliance during import and export processes.

The agent must ensure that all funds received from clients for government dues are deposited promptly into the public treasury and that funds received from the government on behalf of clients are paid to them without delay.
Customs Agents are prohibited from exerting undue influence on customs officials, borrowing money from customs staff, or acting as a guarantor for loans taken by such officials.

The agent must maintain all records, financial documents, bills, and correspondence related to licensing for a minimum period of three years in their office and present them to the customs authority upon request.

Agents are responsible for providing accurate information to clients, notifying customs authorities of any discovered false documentation, and cooperating fully with the customs authorities in the execution of their duties.
Bill of Entry: A Bill of Entry must be submitted electronically or manually, along with appropriate valuation forms, by the Customs Agent after verifying all relevant import documents.
Bill of Export: A Bill of Export must be submitted by the Customs Agent to the customs authority, ensuring that the process remains transparent and that the document is not held in the agent's possession after the customs procedure is completed.
Valuation Rules 2000: Customs Agents must ensure that all declarations for the determination of imported goods' value are prepared and submitted in accordance with the provisions of these rules.
Customs Station: Customs Agents are prohibited from collecting any data or records belonging to the customs authority at a customs station without receiving prior permission from the relevant authorities.
Customs Licensing Authority: The Customs Agent must notify the licensing authority in writing immediately upon any change of their business address.

H.S. Code: Importers are required to clearly specify the H.S. Code for every imported item in their import documentation.
Import Documentation: The importer must include detailed information such as the product description, country of origin, and the H.S. Code on all import documents.
Customs Authority: The customs authority is empowered to demand additional evidence such as printed literature, chemical analysis, and detailed packing lists to verify imported goods.

If the customs authority remains unsatisfied with the submitted documentation, they reserve the right to conduct laboratory testing of the goods in their own facilities or at a government-approved laboratory.

Duty Drawback: Exporters opting for the flat-rate duty drawback system must submit required documentation and data regarding input-output coefficients using the prescribed form before filing an application.
Applicants under the flat-rate duty drawback system are exempted from the requirement to submit import-related documentation for their inputs.

In cases where exporters procure inputs locally that contain embedded import duties, they are not required to submit documentation for either the original import or the local purchase when applying for the drawback.
Exporter: Exporters are responsible for providing all necessary documentation and information to justify input-output coefficients prior to submitting their application for flat-rate duty drawback.

Exporters who procure inputs locally are entitled to apply for duty drawback without submitting individual import or purchase documents, based on the assumption that the purchase price includes paid import duties.

Customs Act 1969: Section 83(C) of the Act serves as the legal basis for issuing official notices to conduct transaction-based audits on imported goods.
Transaction Based Audit: The Audit Team is responsible for conducting a transaction-based audit of specific bills of entry as directed by the Commissioner of Customs.

Auditees are required to present comprehensive documentation regarding their business profile, HS codes, declared values, concessional benefits, and compliance with import policies as part of the audit process.
Commissioner of Customs Valuation and In: This authority or the respective Custom House issues the official notice for the transaction-based audit and oversees the appointment of the audit team.
Import Registration Certificate: Auditees must provide details of their Import Registration Certificate, including its type, to verify their status as industrial or commercial importers.
VAT Compliant: The auditee must submit information confirming their VAT registration status and overall VAT compliance as part of the audit documentation requirements.
H.S. Code: The audit requires verification of declared HS codes against import documents, LCs, and the Bangladesh Customs Tariff, as well as checking against any advance rulings provided by the National Board of Revenue.
National Board of Revenue: The board is responsible for issuing advance rulings on HS codes and granting special concessions or privileges that are subject to review during a customs audit.
Customs Procedure Code: The audit examines concessional benefits claimed under various SROs or special orders to ensure that the appropriate Customs Procedure Code conditions have been satisfied, such as the installation of imported capital machinery.

Transaction Based Audit: This clause provides a comprehensive standard template and guidelines for conducting transaction-based audits of business entities. It outlines required documentation, verification procedures for classification and valuation, and instructions for assessing compliance with import policies and customs duty concessions.
Auditors are instructed to use a risk management approach to randomly sample documents when the volume of bills of entry or other import records is extensive.
H.S. Code: Auditors must verify whether declared HS Codes align with import documents, bills of entry, and letters of credit while ensuring conformity with the Bangladesh Customs Tariff and WCO Explanatory Notes.
Verification includes assessing the application of NBR advance rulings, laboratory reports, and checking for potential misclassification intended to avoid higher duties or import bans.
Exchange Rate: Auditors are required to verify that the correct exchange rates have been applied to imported goods during the assessment process.
Identical Goods: During valuation audits, officers must compare the declared value of imported goods against the value of identical or similar goods imported around the same time to ensure accuracy.
Customs Procedure Code: The audit must verify if goods imported under specific concessional facilities or customs procedure codes comply with all conditions stipulated in the relevant SROs or government orders.
It includes checking if capital machinery imported at a concessional rate is properly installed and if input quantities align with registered production coefficients.
VAT Compliant: Business entities subject to customs audits must be evaluated on whether they maintain VAT compliant status as part of their organizational profile.
Risk Management: When processing large volumes of import documentation, auditors are directed to perform audits based on risk management principles, which involve randomly selecting samples for verification.

System Based Audit: This standing order provides a comprehensive structured checklist for conducting system-based audits of business entities under customs supervision.

Auditors are instructed to evaluate enterprise resource planning data, import-export documentation, valuation compliance, and adherence to specific regulatory rules to identify irregularities or duty evasion.
Authorized Economic Operator: The audit framework requires verification of whether a business entity is registered as an Authorized Economic Operator.
H.S. Code: Auditors must verify that declared HS Codes are consistent with import documents, LCs, BCT, and WCO explanatory notes, and check for misuse of preferential or zero-duty codes.
Risk Management: When dealing with large volumes of bills of entry or documentation, auditors should apply risk management principles to select samples for audit verification.
VAT Compliant: The audit process must confirm the VAT compliant status of the subject entity as part of its operational documentation review.
Manufacturing Process: Auditors are required to verify the manufacturing process, bill of materials, and production flow when examining the ERP or internal software systems of the entity.

System Based Audit: This clause provides a comprehensive checklist and framework for conducting a System Based Audit on business entities involved in customs operations.

The audit framework mandates the verification of organizational data, bonded warehouse compliance, software-based accounting systems, valuation accuracy, and consistency between declared information and actual imports or exports.
Authorized Economic Operator: The audit process requires verification of an Authorized Economic Operator's accreditation status, certificate class, and compliance with the specific conditions required for maintaining their recognition.
H.S. Code: Auditors must ensure that the HS Codes declared on bills of entry match those in import documents and letters of credit, and confirm they are correctly applied according to international explanatory notes and local tariff schedules.
VAT Compliant: The audit process includes verifying whether an entity maintains VAT compliant status, which involves checking their VAT registration, local office records, and overall consistency in tax documentation.
London Metal Exchange: The audit framework directs officers to use data from the London Metal Exchange as an external source to verify the accuracy of metal prices declared by importers.
Platts: Platts is identified as a critical external data source for auditors to cross-verify the international market prices of energy, petrochemicals, metals, and agricultural commodities.
Manufacturing Process: When auditing entities using ERP or other management software, auditors must evaluate the manufacturing module to review bills of materials, work orders, manufacturing capacity, and the actual production flow.
Lock: Auditors are required to investigate the status of Business Identification Number (BIN) locks, including determining whether a lock exists or previously existed and identifying the specific reasons for such enforcement.
Service: The audit includes an assessment of services provided by the business, such as transport or royalty agreements, and checks if these service values are correctly declared and included in the customs valuation.
Exchange Rate: Auditors must verify that the correct exchange rates have been applied to customs declarations and that the declared currency matches the supporting financial documentation.
Materials: The audit process entails verifying the details of raw materials, including their compliance with import policies, description in utilization declarations, and consistency in usage for export-oriented production.
Customs: The document outlines the operational instructions for customs officers to perform structured system-based audits on various business entities to ensure regulatory compliance and revenue protection.
